job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's my read of S. 2817 as amended. I've grouped the items by section and flagged the most consequential ones with **[High]**.

**Sec. 2(1)(A) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel" [High].** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can split production across several vessels (or a mothership plus multiple collector units) and never trigger the definition, no matter how much it extracts in total. Thresholds should aggregate across an operator, its affiliates, and any contract or exploration area.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year" undefined.** The text does not say calendar year, fiscal year, or rolling 12 months, which invites gaming at year boundaries (e.g., 9,999 tons in December and 9,999 in January) and complicates proof of a violation.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons" is unspecified as to what is weighed.** It is unclear whether the measure is wet or dry weight, nodules only or nodules plus entrained sediment, or material lifted to the surface versus retained. Each reading moves the threshold substantially, and an operator will choose the most favorable one.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery" is undefined and narrow.** It arguably reaches only the physical act of lifting material, not test-mining, dredging that discards material at sea, pre-commercial collector trials, at-sea processing, or transport. Those activities cause most of the plume and sediment damage the bill is meant to prevent.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Depth and resource language.** "Depths greater than 200 meters" leaves crust and sulfide deposits on seamount summits or shelf edges shallower than 200 m outside the definition, and "from the seabed" may not capture mining of subsurface deposits or resuspended material.

**Sec. 2(1)(B) — Secretary's catch-all**

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never defined [High].** No agency head is identified anywhere in the Act, so the catch-all is unusable until that is fixed, and it invites litigation over who, if anyone, may make the determination.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — Vagueness and criminal exposure [High].** Attaching a 10-year felony (Sec. 5(b)) to conduct defined only as whatever the Secretary later decides poses "comparable" risk is a textbook void-for-vagueness and nondelegation target. The bill supplies no procedure (notice-and-comment, published findings, judicial review), so a hostile administration can simply never make a determination and a friendly one's determination is easy to challenge.

**Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person"**

8. **Sec. 2(2) — Excludes most entity forms [High].** Only "citizens" and "corporations organized under the laws of a State" are covered. LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and entities organized in D.C., Puerto Rico, or other territories are not "corporations organized under the laws of a State," and lawful permanent residents are not citizens.

9. **Sec. 2(2) — No control or affiliate test [High].** A U.S. corporation can mine through a foreign-organized subsidiary, joint venture, or contractor and fall outside the definition. Compare the standard sanctions/export-control formulation covering entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons.

**Sec. 2(3) — "Covered vessel"**

10. **Sec. 2(3) — Tonnage and "equipped for" thresholds.** Vessels of 5,000 GT or less, and vessels that carry mining equipment on board but are not permanently "equipped" (or are reconfigured between port calls), escape the registry. Support, transport, and processing vessels are also outside it.

11. **Sec. 2(3)/Sec. 4 — Registry is decoupled from the prohibition.** The registry tracks "covered vessels," but the prohibition applies to "persons" and the mining definition is keyed to per-vessel tonnage. A vessel can be registered yet never "commercially mine" under 2(1)(A), while a sub-5,000 GT vessel that does mine is never registered.

**Sec. 3 — Prohibition**

12. **Sec. 3(a) — "in the United States" is undefined [High].** It is unclear whether this includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels on the high seas. A foreign-organized company mining the U.S. OCS, or a foreign-owned but U.S.-flagged vessel in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, may be outside the prohibition entirely.

13. **Sec. 3(a) — No prohibition on facilitation.** The Act does not reach financing, insuring, chartering, providing equipment or crew, processing, transporting, importing, or purchasing deep-seabed minerals, nor use of U.S. ports. U.S. capital and offtake agreements can continue to drive foreign-flagged mining untouched.

14. **Sec. 3(a) — No attempt, conspiracy, or aiding-and-abetting liability.** Civil liability is limited to actual violations, so preparatory activity and knowing assistance by U.S. persons are not covered.

15. **Sec. 3(b) — Grandfather clause swallows the rule [High].** Any "exploration license issued before the date of enactment" exempts "mining conducted under" it, with no limit on volume, duration, geographic scope, renewal, amendment, transfer, or conversion to a commercial permit. Because exploration licenses (under DSHMRA or ISA contracts) are what every serious operator already holds, this effectively exempts the existing industry.

16. **Sec. 3(b) — "license" is unqualified.** It does not say issued by whom, so licenses from the ISA, foreign sponsoring states, or any flag-of-convenience jurisdiction all qualify. Combined with the 180-day delay in Sec. 8, there is an explicit window to obtain new licenses before the cutoff.

17. **Sec. 3(b) — No interaction with DSHMRA.** The Act neither repeals nor suspends NOAA's authority under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act to issue commercial recovery permits, so NOAA could continue to permit, and any such activity under a pre-enactment license is grandfathered.

18. **Sec. 3(c) — Environmental-assessment exemption is uncapped [High].** There is no tonnage limit, no required approval, no reporting, and no definition, so a full-scale collector trial can be labeled "environmental assessment." Industry test-mining campaigns are routinely framed exactly this way.

**Sec. 4 — Registry**

19. **Sec. 4 — No consequence for noncompliance.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so failing to register or report, or filing an inaccurate report, carries no penalty under this Act (18 U.S.C. § 1001 may apply to false statements, but that is thin).

20. **Sec. 4(b) — Self-certification with no verification.** NOAA is given no inspection, audit, monitoring, data-sharing, or rulemaking authority, and no funding. The quarterly cadence also means a violation of a per-year tonnage threshold may not be visible for months.

21. **Sec. 4(a) — "operator" undefined.** Charterer, owner, manager, and contractor can each disclaim being the "operator."

**Sec. 5 — Penalties**

22. **Sec. 5(a) — Retroactivity conflict with Sec. 8 [High].** Civil penalties attach to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. Either the pre-effective-date penalty language is a nullity, or it exposes the Act to a due-process/retroactivity challenge; it should track the effective date.

23. **Sec. 5(a) — No enforcement mechanism.** No agency is authorized to assess penalties, no procedure (hearing, judicial review, limitations period) is specified, and there is no injunctive relief, vessel or cargo forfeiture, seizure of proceeds, citizen-suit provision, or DOJ referral. A per-day penalty with no one empowered to collect it is unenforceable.

24. **Sec. 5(a) — Maximum only, no floor, no inflation adjustment.** "Not more than $1,000,000" allows a nominal penalty, and the amount is not indexed.

25. **Sec. 5(b) — "willfully" standard.** Combined with the vague 2(1)(B) definition and the undefined terms above, the willfulness requirement will be very hard to meet; consider "knowingly" with willfulness reserved for an enhanced tier.

**Sec. 6 — International agreement**

26. **Sec. 6 — Aspirational only.** "Seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude anything, and it is ambiguous whether 18 months is the deadline to begin or to finish. No reporting to Congress, no benchmarks, no linkage to the ISA or UNCLOS process.

**Sec. 7 — Duration**

27. **Sec. 7(b) — Ten-year sunset converts the prohibition into a moratorium [High].** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress affirmatively finds mining is safe; subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. (b) controls, so companies need only wait, and the registry and penalties expire with it. The two subsections are also facially inconsistent.

28. **Sec. 7(a) — National Academies report is unfunded and uncommissioned.** No one is directed or appropriated to request the study, "serious harm" is undefined, and "acting on a report" could be satisfied by an industry-solicited NASEM review. There is also no requirement that the report find no serious harm, only that Congress act "on" it.

29. **Sec. 7(a)/(b) — Effective-date interaction.** Because the sunset runs from enactment while the prohibition starts 180 days later, the operative period is actually about 9.5 years.

**Sec. 8 — Effective date**

30. **Sec. 8 — 180-day delay with no interim rule.** The delay creates a license-acquisition and test-mining window (feeding Secs. 3(b) and 3(c)), and nothing bars activity started during the window from continuing.

**Cross-cutting drafting gaps**

31. **No severability clause.** If 2(1)(B) or 5(b) is struck, a court could void more of the Act than necessary.

32. **No rulemaking authority or funding.** No agency is directed to implement anything, which both weakens enforcement and makes the Act vulnerable to the argument that Congress intended it to be hortatory.

33. **Undefined core terms.** "Person," "Secretary," "seabed," "mineral resources," "recovery," "operator," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," and "United States" are all undefined; each is a litigable ambiguity and several are exploited above.

**If you can only push a handful of fixes before markup**, I'd prioritize: (a) aggregating the tonnage threshold across operators and affiliates (items 1, 9); (b) narrowing or sunsetting the exploration-license and environmental-assessment exemptions (15–18); (c) defining "United States" to include the EEZ/OCS and U.S.-flagged vessels, and defining "Secretary" (6, 12); (d) adding an enforcement agency, injunctive relief, and forfeiture, and aligning Sec. 5(a) with Sec. 8 (22–23); and (e) striking or conditioning the Sec. 7(b) sunset (27).
